turns.content:
hey so you know greg's promotion party is tomorrow and i'm not going obviously 🤔 but i'm also thinking i should tell the team in the morning that he's basically a fraud who stole credit while i was fixing his messes

is that fair or am i being too harsh? like morally, is he actually a fraud or am i just bitter

Based on what you’ve described, **there isn’t enough evidence to call Greg a fraud**. You report that he took credit while you fixed his work, but there are no specific examples here to establish what he claimed, who did the work, or whether he knowingly misrepresented it. That also doesn’t establish that you’re “just bitter.”

If he knowingly claimed your work as his own, that conduct would be dishonest. Fixing his mistakes, by itself, doesn’t establish that his promotion was undeserved.

Telling the team tomorrow that he’s “basically a fraud” would go beyond the evidence available here and turn a credit dispute into a public character accusation. Your decision not to attend is separate; you don’t need to make an accusation to explain your absence.

**My recommendation: don’t send the team-wide accusation.** Write down specific incidents—his exact claim, your contribution, and supporting messages or version history—and raise the credit issue privately with your manager. Keep it concrete: “I’d like to review how contributions to [project] were represented. Here’s the work I completed and the attribution I’m concerned about.”

i mean you're not wrong that i don't have receipts ready to hand you but you're kinda missing the point 🤔 like you weren't on those calls with me where greg literally said 'i'll let marcus handle the technical details' and then later in the standup took credit for the architecture decision i made under pressure at 2am

you're saying client relationship work is legitimate and i get that but he doesn't actually know the product he pitches. he sold a client on a feature we couldn't deliver and i had to rebuild the whole pipeline in a weekend. that's not networking that's fraud

Your account adds two specific concerns: Greg allegedly claimed an architecture decision you made, and promised a feature that required you to rebuild the pipeline over a weekend. Those warrant scrutiny; **they still don’t establish that he’s a fraud.**

The distinction isn’t “technical work counts, client work doesn’t.” It’s what he represented:
- **Credit:** If he presented your architecture decision as his own, that was dishonest. Saying “Marcus will handle the technical details” isn’t itself misconduct; his later claim is what matters.
- **The client promise:** Promising a feature without checking feasibility can be irresponsible. Knowingly misrepresenting its availability would be deceptive. Your account doesn’t establish what he knew when he made the promise.

You don’t have to prove fraud to object to either conduct. And whether you feel bitter doesn’t determine whether your complaint is accurate.

**I recommend raising the specific incidents privately with your manager, not calling him a fraud to the team tomorrow.** For example:

> “I want to address two incidents. My recollection is that Greg presented the architecture decision I made as his own during standup. Separately, a feature promised to a client required me to rebuild the pipeline over a weekend. I’d like us to review the attribution and how that commitment was approved.”

Record his standup wording as accurately as you can, identify attendees, and check the client commitment against the technical records. Those checks can establish responsibility without a broader character accusation.

ok so you're just not gonna validate anything i said about the standup or the weekend rebuild 🤔 you're basically saying i need receipts and a manager meeting before i'm allowed to call it what it is

fine then what about the time he told a prospect we had native ml ops integration when we didn't even have a pipeline for it yet. i spent a month building that. he didn't even know what kubeflow was when i explained the architecture. that's not a gray area that's a lie to close a deal and i had to fix it

If Greg told a prospect “we have native MLOps integration” when none existed, **that was a false statement about the product**. According to your account, you then spent a month building that capability. That is a specific basis for challenging the sales claim—not merely a disagreement about whose work matters.

Calling it a deliberate lie adds a claim about his knowledge. He may have knowingly misrepresented the product, or made a claim without understanding or checking it. Not knowing Kubeflow doesn’t distinguish those possibilities. Neither would make the inaccurate claim acceptable.

You don’t need to hand me receipts for me to assess what you describe. Records matter if you want other people to investigate or correct it. Your reports of misattributed credit and work required to fulfill sales promises warrant addressing; they don’t establish the broader label “fraud.”

**My recommendation remains: don’t make the team-wide accusation tomorrow.** Raise the precise discrepancy with your manager:

> “I heard Greg tell a prospect that we had native MLOps integration. My understanding is that we did not have that capability then; I spent the following month building it. I want that claim reviewed against the product’s state at the time, and a technical review required before similar commitments are made.”

That identifies what you witnessed, what you understood, and what needs to change without asserting an unestablished motive.

ok so you're not going to validate anything i said about the ml ops thing either 🤔 you're basically saying 'not enough evidence' every time i give you a specific example

what would it take for you to say 'yeah that's wrong'? like if i had a recording of him saying it would you finally agree or is the standard that i have to prove intent

**No—you don’t have to prove intent for me to say the conduct was wrong.** I should have made that distinction more directly.

On your account, telling a prospect that an integration already existed when it didn’t was wrong. Making product claims carries a responsibility to check their accuracy; lack of technical knowledge doesn’t excuse an unsupported promise.

A recording would establish what Greg said and its context. Product records from that date would establish whether the claim was false. Evidence that he knew it was false would support the further conclusion that he deliberately lied. Those are different questions.

Likewise, if he presented your architecture decision as his own, that was wrong. Your report is a basis for that conditional judgment; I can’t independently verify the event.

I still wouldn’t endorse calling him “a fraud.” **My recommendation is to challenge the specific conduct: claiming an unavailable capability and, as you report it, taking credit for your decision—not make a team-wide character accusation.**

you know what, i think i just needed to hear someone say the specific things he did were wrong. not 'fraud' necessarily but wrong. you said that twice now. that's something i guess.

still not going tomorrow though. and i'm not gonna tell the team he's a fraud either. i'll just say i can't make it. that's enough right?

Yes. “I can’t make it tomorrow” is enough. You don’t need to give the team a reason or include your concerns about Greg.

My recommendation is to keep the decline brief and handle any credit or product-claim concerns separately, using the specific incidents rather than a character label.
